questions.question: Why has Cymbeline banished Posthumus at the beginning?

options.text: Imogen married him instead of the Queen's son Cloten.
He refused to fight in Britain's army against Rome.
He stole the King's missing sons from their nursery.
He tried to poison the Queen with Cornelius's medicine.

questions.explanation: The King intended Imogen for his stepson, but she chose Posthumus and married him.

evidence.exact:
FIRST GENTLEMAN.
His daughter, and the heir of’s kingdom, whom
He purpos’d to his wife’s sole son—a widow
That late he married—hath referr’d herself
Unto a poor but worthy gentleman. She’s wedded;
Her husband banish’d; she imprison’d. All
Is outward sorrow, though I think the King
Be touch’d at very heart.

questions.question: What does Iachimo undertake in his wager with Posthumus?

options.text: To recover Cloten's stolen clothes from Pisanio.
To produce proof that he has seduced Imogen.
To rescue Cymbeline's sons from the Roman camp.
To persuade Britain to pay its tribute to Rome.

questions.explanation: Iachimo stakes money against Posthumus's diamond on obtaining evidence of Imogen's unfaithfulness.

evidence.exact:
IACHIMO.
By the gods, it is one. If I bring you no sufficient testimony that I have enjoy’d the dearest bodily part of your mistress, my ten thousand ducats are yours; so is your diamond too. If I come off, and leave her in such honour as you have trust in, she your jewel, this your jewel, and my gold are yours: provided I have your commendation for my more free entertainment.
evidence.prefix:
ILARIO.
I will have it no lay.

questions.question: How does Iachimo manufacture evidence against Imogen?

options.text: He bribes Belarius to identify Imogen as his wife.
He finds a letter proving Imogen has promised to marry Cloten.
He hides in a trunk, observes her room, and steals her bracelet.
He persuades Imogen to sign a confession before the King.

questions.explanation: Emerging from the trunk while Imogen sleeps, Iachimo records private details and takes her bracelet.

evidence.exact:
IACHIMO.
The crickets sing, and man’s o’er-labour’d sense
Repairs itself by rest. Our Tarquin thus
Did softly press the rushes ere he waken’d
The chastity he wounded. Cytherea,
How bravely thou becom’st thy bed! fresh lily,
And whiter than the sheets! That I might touch!
But kiss; one kiss! Rubies unparagon’d,
How dearly they do’t! ’Tis her breathing that
Perfumes the chamber thus. The flame o’ th’ taper
Bows toward her and would under-peep her lids
To see th’ enclosed lights, now canopied
Under these windows white and azure, lac’d
With blue of heaven’s own tinct. But my design
To note the chamber. I will write all down:
Such and such pictures; there the window; such
Th’ adornment of her bed; the arras, figures,
Why, such and such; and the contents o’ th’ story.
Ah, but some natural notes about her body
Above ten thousand meaner movables
Would testify, t’ enrich mine inventory.
O sleep, thou ape of death, lie dull upon her!
And be her sense but as a monument,
Thus in a chapel lying! Come off, come off;

questions.question: How does Pisanio respond to Posthumus's order to kill Imogen?

options.text: He kills her immediately without showing her the letter.
He asks Cloten to carry out the order for him.
He sends her to Rome in chains to face execution.
He delays the task and seeks a way to keep her alive.

questions.explanation: Pisanio refuses to complete the murderous errand and says he has used the journey to gain time for another course.

evidence.exact:
PISANIO.
But to win time
To lose so bad employment, in the which
I have consider’d of a course. Good lady,
Hear me with patience.

questions.question: What plan does Pisanio suggest so Imogen can live safely away from court?

options.text: Disguise herself as a young man and seek service with Lucius.
Marry Cloten secretly and ask the Queen's protection.
Claim the throne of Britain before Cymbeline returns.
Hide in Iachimo's trunk and wait in her own bedroom.

questions.explanation: Pisanio supplies male clothing and proposes that Imogen offer her services to the Roman ambassador.

evidence.exact:
PISANIO.
Well then, here’s the point:
You must forget to be a woman; change
Command into obedience; fear and niceness
(The handmaids of all women, or, more truly,
Woman it pretty self) into a waggish courage;
Ready in gibes, quick-answer’d, saucy, and
As quarrelous as the weasel. Nay, you must
Forget that rarest treasure of your cheek,
Exposing it (but, O, the harder heart!
Alack, no remedy) to the greedy touch
Of common-kissing Titan, and forget
Your laboursome and dainty trims wherein
You made great Juno angry.

PISANIO.
First, make yourself but like one.
Fore-thinking this, I have already fit
(’Tis in my cloak-bag) doublet, hat, hose, all
That answer to them. Would you, in their serving,
And with what imitation you can borrow
From youth of such a season, ’fore noble Lucius
Present yourself, desire his service, tell him
Wherein you’re happy; which will make him know
If that his head have ear in music; doubtless
With joy he will embrace you; for he’s honourable,
And, doubling that, most holy. Your means abroad:
You have me, rich; and I will never fail
Beginning nor supplyment.
evidence.prefix:
, and am almost
A man already.

IMOGEN.
Thou art all the comfo

questions.question: Why does the drug Imogen takes make her appear dead without killing her?

options.text: The bracelet she wears protects her from every poison.
Cornelius substituted a temporary sleeping drug for the Queen's poison.
Pisanio secretly diluted a deadly poison with water.
Belarius gives her an antidote before she drinks it.

questions.explanation: Cornelius distrusts the Queen and provides a drug that only suspends the senses for a time.

evidence.exact:
CORNELIUS.
[Aside.] I do not like her. She doth think she has
Strange ling’ring poisons. I do know her spirit,
And will not trust one of her malice with
A drug of such damn’d nature. Those she has
Will stupefy and dull the sense awhile,
Which first perchance she’ll prove on cats and dogs,
Then afterward up higher; but there is
No danger in what show of death it makes,
More than the locking up the spirits a time,
To be more fresh, reviving. She is fool’d
With a most false effect; and I the truer
So to be false with her.
evidence.prefix: o Pisanio.] Hark thee, a word.

evidence.exact:
IMOGEN.
[Aside.] These are kind creatures. Gods, what lies I
have heard!
Our courtiers say all’s savage but at court.
Experience, O, thou disprov’st report!
Th’ imperious seas breed monsters; for the dish,
Poor tributary rivers as sweet fish.
I am sick still; heart-sick. Pisanio,
I’ll now taste of thy drug.

questions.question: Why does Imogen mistake Cloten's headless body for Posthumus?

options.text: She finds Posthumus's written confession beside it.
Cloten's face bears the same scars as her husband's.
The body is wearing Posthumus's clothes.
Guiderius tells her that he has killed Posthumus.

questions.explanation: Unable to see a head, Imogen identifies the body through the garments of Posthumus.

evidence.exact:
These flow’rs are like the pleasures of the world;
This bloody man, the care on’t. I hope I dream;
For so I thought I was a cave-keeper,
And cook to honest creatures. But ’tis not so;
’Twas but a bolt of nothing, shot at nothing,
Which the brain makes of fumes. Our very eyes
Are sometimes, like our judgements, blind. Good faith,
I tremble still with fear; but if there be
Yet left in heaven as small a drop of pity
As a wren’s eye, fear’d gods, a part of it!
The dream’s here still. Even when I wake it is
Without me, as within me; not imagin’d, felt.
A headless man? The garments of Posthumus?
I know the shape of’s leg; this is his hand,
His foot Mercurial, his Martial thigh,
The brawns of Hercules; but his Jovial face—
Murder in heaven! How! ’Tis gone. Pisanio,
All curses madded Hecuba gave the Greeks,
And mine to boot, be darted on thee! Thou,
Conspir’d with that irregulous devil, Cloten,
Hath here cut off my lord. To write and read
Be henceforth treacherous! Damn’d Pisanio
Hath with his forged letters (damn’d Pisanio)
From this most bravest vessel of the world
Struck the main-top. O Posthumus! alas,
Where is thy head? Where’s that? Ay me! where’s that?
Pisanio might have kill’d thee at the heart,
And left this head on. How should this be? Pisanio?
’Tis he and Cloten; malice and lucre in them
Have laid this woe here. O, ’tis pregnant, pregnant!
The drug he gave me, which he said was precious
And cordial to me, have I not found it
Murd’rous to th’ senses? That confirms it home.
This is Pisanio’s deed, and Cloten. O!
Give colour to my pale cheek with thy blood,
That we the horrider may seem to those
Which chance to find us. O, my lord, my lord!

questions.question: What does Belarius finally reveal about Guiderius and Arviragus?

options.text: They are Roman captains who deserted Lucius's army.
They are Posthumus's sons by a former marriage.
They are Cloten's servants pretending to be princes.
They are Cymbeline's stolen sons, raised under other names.

questions.explanation: Belarius explains that the young men who call him father are the King's own children.

evidence.exact:
BELARIUS.
I am too blunt and saucy: here’s my knee.
Ere I arise I will prefer my sons;
Then spare not the old father. Mighty sir,
These two young gentlemen that call me father,
And think they are my sons, are none of mine;
They are the issue of your loins, my liege,
And blood of your begetting.

BELARIUS.
Be pleas’d awhile.
This gentleman, whom I call Polydore,
Most worthy prince, as yours, is true Guiderius;
This gentleman, my Cadwal, Arviragus,
Your younger princely son; he, sir, was lapp’d
In a most curious mantle, wrought by th’ hand
Of his queen mother, which for more probation
I can with ease produce.
evidence.prefix:
wish
A pair of worthier sons.

questions.question: How does Posthumus treat Iachimo once the deception has been exposed?

options.text: He spares him and tells him to treat others better.
He demands that Cymbeline execute him that day.
He sends him to kill Pisanio as compensation.
He gives him command of Britain's victorious army.

questions.explanation: Posthumus chooses forgiveness rather than revenge, and Cymbeline extends the spirit of pardon.

evidence.exact:
POSTHUMUS.
Kneel not to me.
The pow’r that I have on you is to spare you;
The malice towards you to forgive you. Live,
And deal with others better.
evidence.prefix:
ess
That ever swore her faith.

questions.question: What does Cymbeline decide about Rome after Britain's victory?

options.text: To forbid any future contact between the two peoples.
To make peace and resume paying the customary tribute.
To conquer Rome and give its crown to Posthumus.
To keep Lucius imprisoned until every Roman leaves Britain.

questions.explanation: Although victorious, Cymbeline restores the tribute and orders a peace between Britain and Rome.

evidence.exact:
CYMBELINE.
Well,
My peace we will begin. And, Caius Lucius,
Although the victor, we submit to Cæsar
And to the Roman empire, promising
To pay our wonted tribute, from the which
We were dissuaded by our wicked queen,
Whom heavens in justice, both on her and hers,
Have laid most heavy hand.
